summary: Defines an information model for the Measurement Agent in a Large-Scale Measurement Platform. It describes what is configured on the agent and what is exchanged with a Controller or Collector, in a way independent of protocol and device.

plainLanguage.summary: A checklist describing everything a measuring gadget needs to know and report, no matter the brand.

questions: what is a measurement agent in lmap
what is the lmap information model
what is a schedule in lmap
subtitle: A protocol-neutral description of what a measurement device is told to do, what it reports, and how it is scheduled.

tldr.problem: Large-scale measurement platforms run tests from many vantage points such as home gateways, but without a shared description of what a Measurement Agent holds and exchanges, control and report protocols cannot be compared or made to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an information model in six groups (preconfiguration, configuration, instruction, logging, capability and status, reporting), built on common objects: Schedules, Actions, Channels, Task Configurations and Events.
tldr.outcome: The model guides Control and Report protocols and data models. A YANG data model implementing it is given in RFC 8194.

today: RFC 8193 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata, and its YANG data model counterpart is RFC 8194.

sections.title: The Measurement Platform and Its Parts
sections.content:
A large-scale measurement platform runs measurements from many vantage points; a typical use is broadband measurement (RFC 7536). It has three kinds of component: Measurement Agents (MAs) that perform the measurements, Controllers that instruct them, and Collectors that gather the results. An MA is controlled by exactly one Controller at a time. The overall framework is in RFC 7594.

Three kinds of protocol are involved: a Control Protocol between Controller and MA, a Report Protocol between MA and Collector, and measurement protocols between the MA and Measurement Peers. This document models the Control and Report Protocols plus the preconfiguration an MA needs before it contacts a Controller. Measurement protocols are out of scope.

It is an information model in the sense of RFC 3444: a high-level abstraction independent of any protocol or device, whether a home gateway, smartphone, PC or router. A YANG data model that implements it is in RFC 8194.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of little gadgets run speed tests. A boss tells them what to test, and a collector gathers their answers. This document describes the instructions and answers in a way any brand can follow.

sections.title: The Six Kinds of Information
sections.content:
The model groups what an MA holds or exchanges into six aspects. The grouping helps readers, and the groups are expected to map to different protocols or different transmissions within them.

  • Preconfiguration: what the MA has before talking to anyone, mainly how to reach a Controller and whether the device may act as an MA.
  • Configuration: updates to that during registration, plus further facts about the MA itself.
  • Instruction: what the Controller tells the MA to do: Schedules, Task Configurations, Report Channels and Suppression.
  • Logging: results of configuration operations and error and status messages sent to the Controller.
  • Capability and Status: what the MA can do and what it has done lately.
  • Reporting: measurement results and their context, sent to Collectors.

The model does not dictate how much data a protocol sends in one operation, whether data is read, write or read/write, or whether a protocol overwrites everything or updates selected items. The notation is a simple programming-like object syntax in which [ ] marks an optional property and <m..n> a list.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like sorting the gadget's paperwork into six folders: what it knew at the factory, its settings, its to-do list, its diary, its skills list, and its answer sheets.

sections.title: Schedules, Actions, Tasks and Events
sections.content:
Everything the MA does is driven by Schedules. Without a Schedule, no Task is ever executed, including measuring, reporting or contacting the Controller. Four kinds of common object support them:

  • Schedule: an Event that triggers it plus an ordered list of Actions. A specific Schedule can only be active once; trying to start it while it still runs fails.
  • Action: a configured Task with extra Options, and optionally Destination Schedules that receive its output.
  • Task Configuration: the parameters of a Task, with registry entries that let the MA identify and resolve it. By itself it does not make anything run.
  • Channel: the target location and security details for a single endpoint, a Controller or a Collector.

Tasks fall into categories: Measurement Tasks, Data Transfer Tasks (Reporting Tasks and Control Tasks), Data Analysis Tasks and Data Management Tasks. In the model all Tasks have the same structure.

A Schedule runs its Actions in sequential, parallel or pipelined mode, and the default is pipelined, where data from one Action goes to the next. Schedules with the same start time run in parallel, and there is no mechanism to prioritize one or to mutex Tasks. Data fed to a Destination Schedule is consumed by the first Action in sequential or pipelined mode, and by all Actions in parallel mode.
sections.plainLanguage: A schedule is like a chore chart: at this time, do these jobs in this order, and hand the results to this other chart. Without a chart the gadget does nothing at all.

sections.title: Instructions, Suppression and Reporting
sections.content:
The Instruction has four parts: Task Configurations, Report Channels, Schedules and Suppression. They are separate so each can change without disturbing the others. Channels and Task Configurations are expected to be fairly static, while Schedules change more often as the measurement panel and test frequency change.

Suppression temporarily overrides the Schedules. It uses tags and glob-style patterns (following POSIX.2 fnmatch) to match Schedules or Actions, and it can optionally stop running Tasks as well as new ones. Control Schedules and Tasks cannot be suppressed. It is ended by overwriting it or by giving it an end time.

Reporting. A Reporting Task sends results over a Report Channel to a Collector. Output does not have to go to a Channel; it can be fed to other Tasks, so one measurement can steer a later one or trigger local alarms. A report is structured hierarchically, starting with a timestamp and the optional MA identifier and Group-ID, and much of the rest is optional. A Reporting Task may send just the header when no data is available.

The MA also keeps Logging messages (for example a failure to parse an instruction) and exposes Capability and Status information such as hardware, firmware, supported Tasks, interfaces and per-Schedule counters for invocations, suppressions, overlaps and failures.
sections.plainLanguage: A pause button lets the boss stop some tests quickly without rewriting the chore chart. When the pause ends, the old chart still works.

sections.title: Events and Timing
sections.content:
Every Schedule references exactly one Event that decides when it runs. The initial Event forms are:

  • Periodic timing, at an interval in seconds
  • Calendar timing, such as 22 minutes past each hour on weekdays
  • One-off timing at a specific date and time
  • Immediate
  • Startup, when the MA starts
  • Controller Lost, when connectivity to the Controller is lost
  • Controller Connected, when connectivity is established or re-established

Each Event may carry a randomness value, a uniform interval in seconds over which the start is delayed. Periodic and calendar timing can run a series of Actions. Both have an optional end time, but the best practice is to always set one and refresh it, so that lost MAs do not run Tasks forever.

Startup Events occur only on device startup, not when a new Instruction arrives. To run on both, use Immediate and Startup together. All datetime values MUST follow RFC 3339.
sections.plainLanguage: Events are the alarm clocks. Some ring every so often, some ring once, and one rings when the gadget loses touch with its boss.

sections.title: Bootstrapping and Control Channels
sections.content:
An MA needs minimal preconfiguration to register with a Controller: the Controller's URL and the security information to talk to it, including the Controller's certificate or the certificate of the Certification Authority that issued it, all expressed as a Channel. When the MA pulls from the Controller, a Schedule triggered by an Event runs the Control Task. When the Controller pushes, a Schedule still runs a Controller listener Task at start.

The MA may have an MA-ID preconfigured or use a Device ID, such as a MAC address expressed as a URI, for first contact. If it has no MA-ID, the Controller MUST supply one during configuration. A Group-ID may also be assigned, and flags decide whether the MA-ID, Group-ID or measurement point appears in reports. Reporting only a Group-ID may keep an MA anonymous, which helps prevent tracking of mobile devices.

As a fail-safe, an MA can be told to stop Instruction Schedules when the Controller is unreachable. A timer started at each successful contact raises a Controller Lost Event when it reaches the configured timeout in seconds. Preconfiguration persists across reset or power cycle, while persistence of Configuration is device dependent.
sections.plainLanguage: A new gadget is given the boss's address and a badge to prove who it is. If it cannot reach the boss for too long, it can stop its jobs rather than follow stale orders.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
There are two main concerns. First, the model must be enough to set up secure Channels to the Controller and Collector, and whatever mechanism a network operator uses to preconfigure the MA must itself be secure, so that the MA cannot be hijacked, for example to join a distributed denial-of-service attack.

Second, no mandated item should threaten confidentiality or privacy. For this reason items such as the MA context and the MA-ID are optional and can be left out of some deployments, and deployments should be careful about exposing device IDs. Implementers should follow the security and privacy requirements of the LMAP framework (RFC 7594) and choose Group-IDs, tags and object names that do not reveal sensitive information to people who may read results but should not know about the specific agents. The document needs no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The gadget must not be tricked into taking orders from strangers, and its labels should not give away who or where it is.

items.title: Preconfiguration
items.text: How to reach the first Controller, set before any contact.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: Updates to that plus MA identity details.

items.title: Instruction
items.text: Tasks, Schedules, Channels and Suppression from the Controller.

items.title: Logging
items.text: Success, failure and status messages to the Controller.

items.title: Capability and Status
items.text: What the MA supports and when it last acted.

items.title: Reporting
items.text: Results and context sent to Collectors.
